title: Live Triage Simulation: Cyber Hero Shift
summary: A full simulated support shift built around 8 tickets of escalating difficulty: a blocked legitimate app, suspected malware, an elevation request, a storage-control false positive, a network-control outage, a Detect alert, an angry customer, and an executive escalation. You triage under time pressure, resolve each ticket against a scored rubric, and compare your resolutions to model answers.
objectives: Triage incoming endpoint-security tickets by severity, business impact, and security risk within minutes.
Distinguish legitimate-application blocks from genuine malware using allowlisting investigation steps.
Resolve elevation, storage, and network-control tickets without weakening the zero-trust posture.
Handle Detect alerts, angry customers, and executive escalations with professional, de-escalating communication.
Document every action so a teammate could take over your queue cold.

notes.title: How a zero-trust support shift actually runs
notes.body:
A support shift in a zero-trust environment is a queue discipline, not heroics. Tickets arrive from users, automated alerts, and phone calls; each gets a severity (how bad is the impact), an urgency (how fast it needs action), and an owner (you). Worked example: three tickets land at once: (1) a nurse can't open a charting app because allowlisting blocked it, (2) a Detect alert fired on a workstation, (3) a developer wants local admin for a tool install. You triage in this order: the Detect alert first (potential active threat — seconds matter), the nurse second (business impact on patient care — minutes matter), the developer last (a request, not an incident — hours are fine). Your rule: threats beat outages, outages beat friction, friction beats requests. Every ticket gets three artifacts: what you observed, what you did, and why you did it — written as you go, never reconstructed from memory. A common operator gotcha: starting work on the loudest ticket instead of the most severe. The angry customer who calls twice still loses to the silent malware alert you haven't looked at. Timebox investigation: 10 minutes to classify, then either resolve, escalate, or contain. Document your handoff state even when nobody is taking over — future-you at hour six of the shift is a different person who needs those notes.

A concrete documentation habit makes this real. Use a fixed ticket-entry format: TIME | TICKET | OBSERVED | ACTION | REASON | NEXT. Worked example: 09:42 | #4821 | Detect alert: powershell.exe spawned from winword.exe on WS-114, IOC match on known malicious hash | Isolated WS-114 from network, preserved memory image to share | Process tree matches credential-access pattern; isolation prevents lateral movement | Awaiting security-lead review before reimage. That entry takes 60 seconds and lets anyone take over. Second worked example — SLA math: your team promises 4-hour response on high-priority blocks. A ticket opened at 09:00 with first action at 09:42 is fine; the same ticket untouched until 13:30 is a breach. Track your oldest untouched ticket, not your total count — queues die from the oldest ticket, not the newest. Operator gotcha: documenting only resolutions. The dead ends matter too: 'checked policy P-CLIN-04, not the cause' saves the next person 20 minutes. End-of-shift handoff is three lines: what's still open, what's waiting on someone else, and the one thing you'd investigate first tomorrow. Write it even when nobody asks — the discipline is the skill.

notes.title: Ticket 1 & 2: blocked legit app vs suspected malware
notes.body:
Allowlisting denies by default, so blocked legitimate applications are the most common ticket in a ThreatLocker environment — and the most dangerous to mis-handle, because the fix for a false positive (approve the app) looks identical to the mistake that lets malware run (approve the wrong app). Worked example: a user reports that invoicing-software setup.exe was blocked. Your investigation: (1) identify the file — hash it (PowerShell: Get-FileHash setup.exe -Algorithm SHA256) and record the path, signer, and publisher; (2) check policy — which allowlisting policy covers this machine and does it permit this hash or publisher; (3) verify legitimacy — is this the vendor's expected binary (compare hash against the vendor's published checksum if available), was it downloaded from the vendor's site, does the business actually use this software; (4) decide — approve by hash or publisher rule if legitimate, quarantine and investigate if not. Now contrast Ticket 2: a workstation shows a Detect alert on payroll-helper.exe phoning an external IP. Same shape, opposite conclusion: unknown binary, no business justification, network beaconing. Here you do NOT approve — you isolate the machine from the network, preserve memory and logs before reimaging (see forensics fundamentals), and escalate to the security lead. The operator gotcha that fails interviews: approving a block exception by filename. Filenames lie; hashes don't. Always approve on hash or verified publisher, scoped to the smallest set of machines, never fleet-wide on day one.

Second worked example — the hash-mismatch catch: a user reports blocked installer for the vendor's PDF tool. You hash it: SHA256 a91f... The vendor's published checksum is 4c22... Mismatch. Investigation: the user downloaded it from a lookalike domain (vendor-support-download.com instead of vendor.com). Decision: deny, quarantine the file, and treat the workstation as potentially compromised — scan and check Detect history. That single hash comparison just stopped a trojanized installer. Decision tree for approvals: vendor-signed with valid chain plus expected publisher name goes to publisher-rule approval; unsigned or hash-mismatched goes to quarantine-and-investigate; hash matches vendor published checksum goes to hash approval. Another gotcha: learning mode versus enforced mode. In learning mode the agent observes without blocking — perfect for baselining, useless for protection. Know which mode each machine is in before you promise a user 'it's fixed'; an approval in learning mode changes nothing visible. And when you approve, record the ticket number in the policy change note — six months later, someone auditing that rule needs to know why it exists.

notes.title: Ticket 3: elevation requests without local admin
notes.body:
Elevation Control removes local admin and grants just-in-time elevation to applications via policy — so your job on an elevation ticket is to satisfy a legitimate need without recreating the local-admin problem. Worked example: a developer needs to run docker-desktop installer, which requires elevation. Your workflow: (1) verify the person — is this their normal role and machine; (2) verify the artifact — hash the installer, confirm it came from the vendor; (3) scope the grant — elevate the installer only, not the user's session, and only on their machine; (4) time-bound it — the elevation applies to this install event, not permanently; (5) log it — who, what hash, when, why, ticket number. The decision framework: what (exact binary), why (business justification), how long (single execution vs recurring), where (which machines). Common mistakes: elevating the user instead of the application (that hands back the keys you're paid to hold), granting fleet-wide when one machine asked, and approving from a phone call without verifying identity — elevation requests are a classic social-engineering vector. If the request is recurring (a weekly report tool that needs elevation every Monday), that's a policy-design signal: propose a standing application-elevation rule for that binary rather than a weekly ticket. Track elevation grants per week; a rising trend means your baseline policies need tuning, not that users are needier.

Worked example of the recurring pattern: every Monday, the reporting tool needs elevation to refresh its data connector. Three Mondays of tickets later, you propose the standing rule: elevate report-refresh.exe (hash-pinned) on the finance machines, logged, reviewed quarterly. Ticket volume drops, users stop resenting the control, and the security posture is identical — better, actually, because the rule is narrower than three ad-hoc grants. Red flags that should freeze an elevation request: the requester can't name the business purpose, the binary arrived by email attachment, the request comes from a different machine than the requester's normal one, or there's urgency pressure ('the CEO needs this in five minutes'). Any one of those converts the ticket from 'grant' to 'verify identity and investigate.' The social-engineering angle is real: attackers know the helpdesk can grant elevation, so your verification script matters — call back on a known number, confirm via the ticket system, never approve from a cold call alone. Log every grant with the four scoping answers; quarterly, review the grant log for patterns — five grants for the same binary means a missing policy rule, and one grant at 2 AM means a conversation.

notes.title: Ticket 4: storage-control false positive vs real exfiltration
notes.body:
Storage Control governs storage devices, file paths, and shares — so its tickets split into two buckets that demand opposite responses: legitimate workflow friction and actual data theft. Worked example: a clinic's billing clerk plugs in an encrypted USB drive to transfer month-end reports and Storage Control blocks all writes. Investigation: is the drive the clinic's issued encrypted device or a personal one? Is the destination a sanctioned path? If the clerk is doing approved month-end work on a personal drive, the fix is a scoped exception — allow this device class for this user group to these paths, time-bound to month-end — not a permanent 'allow all USB.' Contrast the exfiltration pattern: a departing employee copies the client database to a personal drive at 11 PM. Indicators that flip your posture: off-hours timing, bulk copy of sensitive directories, personal hardware, and resignation/HR context. In that case you don't tune policy — you preserve the evidence trail (block logs, file-access records), notify your lead, and follow the incident response path. The gotcha: users will always describe a block as 'I was just doing my job.' Take that seriously but verify independently — check the block details (device ID, paths, volume) against the stated workflow before touching policy. Every exception gets an owner, an expiry, and a review date; exceptions without expiries become permanent holes with extra steps.

Second worked example — reading a bulk-copy pattern: Storage Control logs show 14 GB copied from the patient-records share to an unrecognized USB device at 22:40 by a user whose shift ended at 17:00. Compare with the legitimate pattern: the same user copies 200 MB to the clinic-issued encrypted drive at 16:30 on month-end days. Volume, timing, device identity, and destination all differ — that's your exfiltration signal, and your action is preserve-and-escalate, not policy-tune. Device-class thinking helps: maintain three classes — clinic-issued encrypted (allowed with scoping), approved vendor devices (case-by-case), personal/unknown (default deny). When the clinic buys new encrypted drives, the exception isn't 'allow USB' — it's 'add these device IDs to the clinic-issued class.' The human conversation matters too: when you deny a personal drive, explain the alternative in the same breath ('use the clinic drive from the front desk — here's where to get one'). Users circumvent controls they experience as pure obstruction; they comply with controls that come with a working path. Document every storage exception with the data classification involved — patient-data paths get your sign-off, not just the IT generalist's.

notes.title: Ticket 5: when network control IS the incident
notes.body:
Network Control is an endpoint firewall with dynamic ACLs that open and close ports — powerful against lateral movement and command-and-control, and fully capable of causing the outage you're asked to fix. Worked example: after a policy push, three finance workstations lose access to the shared accounting drive. Your diagnosis order: (1) confirm scope — is it these three machines only, or the server side too; (2) check what changed — pull the recent policy change log and its timestamp against the outage start; (3) test the hypothesis — does the new network policy's allowed-port set include the file-share traffic (SMB) these workstations need; (4) remediate surgically — adjust the ACL for the finance group rather than disabling Network Control; (5) verify — confirm connectivity restored and that the blocked lateral-movement protections still hold elsewhere. The discipline here is change correlation: in a deny-by-default world, 'it worked yesterday' almost always means 'a policy changed.' Keep a personal rule: never disable a control module to restore service. You narrow the policy, you don't turn it off — because the minute you disable Network Control fleet-wide to fix finance, you've removed the lateral-movement barrier everywhere. If the fix isn't obvious in 15 minutes, roll back the specific policy change and investigate offline; uptime for the business beats elegance of the root cause. Document the policy diff that fixed it — that's your change record.

Worked example with ports: the accounting share breaks after a Network Control push. You check the finance tier's ACL: allowed destinations are the file server on TCP 445 (SMB) and the print server on 9100. The new policy version dropped the 445 rule — someone 'cleaned up' the rule set. Fix: restore the explicit 445 allow for file-server-only, scoped to the finance tier, with a change note referencing the ticket. Verification is two-sided: confirm the share works AND confirm workstation-to-workstation traffic is still denied (test from one finance machine to another — it should fail). Rollback runbook, written before you need it: identify the policy version that broke things, revert to the previous known-good version for the affected tier only, verify service restoration, then diagnose the bad change offline. Never roll back the entire fleet for one tier's problem. Change windows matter: push network policy changes in evening windows with a verification checklist (file shares, printing, backup, authentication) — the four workflows that break most often. And keep a one-page network map of tier-to-tier allowed flows; when the 2 AM call comes, you diagnose from the map, not from memory.

notes.title: Ticket 6 & 7: Detect alerts and the angry customer
notes.body:
Detect alerts on indicators of compromise blocked by the modules; your triage decides whether the block was the whole story or the first chapter. Worked example: Detect fires on a workstation — blocked process injection from a browser helper. Your triage: (1) read the alert fully — which module blocked it, what process tree, what IOC; (2) assess — known-bad indicator or heuristic, single machine or several; (3) contain if warranted — isolate the host from the network while you look; (4) decide the story — commodity adware blocked cleanly (close with notes) vs a pattern across machines (escalate as a possible incident). Never assume a blocked alert is a closed case; a blocked initial attempt is often followed by a second one. Now Ticket 7, the angry customer: their words will be about your product ('your software is broken'), but the underlying emotion is fear of looking incompetent in front of their boss. De-escalation script: acknowledge impact first ('I understand this blocked you during the client presentation — let's get you working'), then diagnose aloud so they hear competence ('I can see the block was our allowlisting policy on this installer — let me verify it and get it approved'), then resolve and confirm ('it's approved now — please retry while I'm on the line'). The gotcha: arguing about who's right while the customer is down. Fix first, explain second, educate never — nobody learns policy architecture while angry. After resolution, a one-line plain-language explanation of why the block happened turns the angry customer into the one who defends the control next time.

Second worked example — the pattern that becomes an incident: three Detect alerts in one morning, all blocked process injection from the same browser helper version, on three different machines. Individually each looks like adware blocked cleanly. Together they're a campaign — same initial vector, same hour. Your move: escalate as a suspected incident, pull the browser helper's deployment history (was it pushed yesterday?), and check whether unblocked machines show the same process tree. The model resolution for Ticket 6 isn't 'closed three alerts' — it's 'correlated, escalated, and found the pushed update.' For the angry customer, the follow-up that converts them: a short email after resolution — what was blocked, why the control exists (one sentence, plain language), and what you changed so it won't recur. Template: 'Hi [name], following up on today's block: our allowlisting stopped an unrecognized installer from running, which is exactly what it's for — but it shouldn't have hit your legitimate tool. I've approved it for your team so this won't happen again. If anything else gets blocked, call me directly.' That email takes two minutes and turns today's complaint into tomorrow's reference story.

notes.title: Ticket 8: executive escalation and the scoring rubric
notes.body:
Executive escalations are ordinary tickets wearing expensive suits: same technical work, different communication wrapper. Worked example: the CFO's laptop is blocked from running a board-presentation tool 40 minutes before a board meeting. Technical handling is identical to Ticket 1 — verify the binary, approve by hash, scope to the machine. What changes is cadence and framing: update every 10 minutes even if the update is 'still verifying the file,' speak in business impact ('you'll be able to present at 2:00 — the file checks out clean'), and never say 'policy says no' without the next sentence being the path to yes. Afterward, write the incident summary in executive language: what happened, what you did, how long, and what prevents recurrence. Now the scoring rubric for this whole shift simulation — how your resolutions are judged: correctness of the technical decision (did you approve/deny/isolate the right thing — 40%), security posture preserved (did you avoid weakening controls to buy speed — 25%), communication quality (did the user know what was happening — 20%), documentation (could someone audit your shift — 15%). Timeboxing matters: a perfect resolution delivered after the SLA is a partial score. The model resolutions at the end of this module show the 100-point version of each ticket — compare yours honestly, note where you traded posture for speed, and re-run any ticket you scored below 70 on.

Worked example of the executive summary write-up for Ticket 8: 'At 13:20, the CFO's board-presentation tool was blocked by our application allowlisting (unrecognized binary). I verified the file hash against the vendor, confirmed it was legitimate, and approved it for the CFO's laptop at 13:31. The presentation proceeded on schedule. Root cause: the tool was updated yesterday and the new version wasn't in our approved set. Prevention: I've added the vendor's publisher certificate to the executive tier policy so future updates won't block.' Four sentences: what, what you did, how long, prevention. Now score yourself on Ticket 3 (elevation) as a rubric example: correctness — did you scope to the binary, not the session? (40 points possible) Posture — is there an expiry and a log entry, no local admin granted? (25) Communication — does the user know when the elevation applies and what to do next time? (20) Documentation — could an auditor reconstruct the grant? (15). A resolution that grants correctly but forgets the log entry scores 85 — good, not perfect, and the missing 15 is exactly the habit to build. Re-run any ticket under 70 with the model resolution open beside you, then close it and re-run once more from memory.

quiz.q: Three tickets land: a Detect alert, a blocked charting app, and an admin-rights request. What order?
choices: Detect alert, charting app, admin request
Charting app, Detect alert, admin request
Admin request first — it's quickest
Whoever called loudest goes first
quiz.explain: Threats beat outages, outages beat friction, friction beats requests. The alert could be active malicious activity; the app is business impact; the request is neither.

quiz.q: A user needs setup.exe approved. What is the correct basis for approval?
choices: Approve by filename across the fleet
Approve by hash or verified publisher, scoped narrowly
Disable allowlisting for their department for the day
Tell them to rename it and try again
quiz.explain: Filenames are attacker-controlled; hash or verified publisher proves identity. Narrow scoping limits blast radius if you're wrong.

quiz.q: Payroll-helper.exe is beaconing to an external IP per Detect. First action?
choices: Approve it so payroll runs
Isolate the host from the network, then investigate
Reimage immediately to stop it
Wait to see if it happens again
quiz.explain: Contain first to stop potential spread or exfiltration, but preserve memory/logs before reimaging — evidence dies with the reimage.

quiz.q: A developer needs to run an installer requiring elevation. Best practice?
choices: Grant their account local admin for the day
Elevate the installer binary only, on their machine, for this install
Have them install it on a server instead
Deny — developers should never install software
quiz.explain: Elevation Control exists to elevate applications, not users. Scoping to the binary and the event preserves least privilege.

quiz.q: Month-end USB block for a billing clerk. The drive is personal, not clinic-issued. Best response?
choices: Permanent allow-all-USB exception for billing
Scoped, time-bound exception for the workflow — and flag the personal-drive policy issue
Disable Storage Control until month-end passes
Tell the clerk to email the files to themselves
quiz.explain: Solve the immediate workflow with a narrow, expiring exception while noting the policy gap (personal drives with financial data) for review — not a permanent hole.

quiz.q: After a policy push, finance loses file-share access. Most likely cause?
choices: The file server's disk failed at the same time
The new network policy's ACL no longer permits the share traffic
Users forgot their passwords simultaneously
Allowlisting blocked the accounting application
quiz.explain: In deny-by-default environments, 'worked yesterday, broken today' correlates with policy changes. Check the change log against the outage start time.

quiz.q: You can't find the Network Control misconfiguration within 15 minutes. What now?
choices: Disable Network Control fleet-wide until you figure it out
Roll back the specific policy change, restore service, investigate offline
Keep digging — uptime can wait for a root cause
Ask finance to work without the share today
quiz.explain: Roll back the specific change to restore service, then investigate without the outage clock running. Never trade a fleet-wide control for one team's access.

quiz.q: An angry customer says your software broke their presentation. First sentence out of your mouth should:
choices: Explain the allowlisting policy architecture
Acknowledge the impact and commit to getting them working
Ask them to calm down
Blame the policy their admin configured
quiz.explain: Impact first, diagnosis second. People can't hear explanations while they're down; competence is demonstrated by fixing, then explaining.

quiz.q: The CFO is blocked 40 minutes before a board meeting. How often do you update them?
choices: Only when fully resolved
About every 10 minutes, even if the update is 'still verifying'
Every 2 minutes
Have their assistant check back later
quiz.explain: Executives escalate on silence, not slowness. A steady cadence of honest updates keeps the escalation from growing while you do the same technical work.

quiz.q: Under the shift rubric, which factor carries the most weight?
choices: Speed of resolution
Correctness of the technical decision (40%)
Length of documentation
Customer satisfaction survey
quiz.explain: A fast wrong answer (approving malware) is catastrophic; correctness dominates, with posture preservation second. Speed matters through SLA timeboxing, not as the top score.

items.prompt: Severity ordering: threats, outages, friction, requests.
items.answer: Threats > outages > friction > requests.
items.explain: Risk to the business decides the queue, not volume or loudness.

items.prompt: Timebox for initial ticket classification?
items.answer: About 10 minutes: resolve, escalate, or contain.
items.explain: Classification must be fast; deep investigation follows for the tickets that earn it.

items.prompt: Block-approval basis: filename, hash, or publisher?
items.answer: Hash or verified publisher.
items.explain: Filenames are trivially spoofed by malware.

items.prompt: Elevation granted to user session or application?
items.answer: Application only.
items.explain: Elevating the session recreates the local-admin risk Elevation Control removed.

items.prompt: Every exception needs which three properties?
items.answer: An owner, an expiry, and a review date.
items.explain: Exceptions without expiries become permanent holes with extra steps.

items.prompt: A blocked Detect alert with no other signs — close it?
items.answer: Not automatically — check for follow-up attempts and cross-machine patterns first.
items.explain: Blocked first attempts are often followed by second attempts.

items.prompt: Network outage right after a policy push — first check?
items.answer: The policy change log correlated with outage start time.
items.explain: Deny-by-default makes policy changes the prime suspect for new breakage.

items.prompt: Forbidden shortcut when a control blocks legitimate work?
items.answer: Disabling the control module.
items.explain: Narrow the policy; never turn off the control.

items.prompt: Ticket: HR's onboarding app blocked by allowlisting, 12 new hires waiting. Your first two actions?
items.answer: Verify the binary (hash, source, publisher), then approve narrowly scoped to HR machines.
items.explain: Business impact is real, but verification comes before approval — same workflow as Ticket 1, executed fast.

items.prompt: Ticket: Detect flags a macro-enabled spreadsheet email attachment that was blocked. User insists it's from a client. Action?
items.answer: Do not approve from the user's word. Verify sender independently, inspect the file safely, treat as suspected phishing until proven otherwise.
items.explain: Malicious attachments routinely arrive as 'expected client files.' User assurance is not verification.

items.prompt: Ticket: IT admin requests standing elevation for a patching tool used weekly. One-time grant or policy rule?
items.answer: Propose a standing application-elevation policy rule for that binary — recurring needs are policy-design signals.
items.explain: Weekly tickets for the same binary mean the baseline policy is incomplete; fix the policy, not the symptom.

items.prompt: Ticket: Storage Control blocks a developer copying a repo to an external SSD. Legit workflow. Fix shape?
items.answer: Scoped exception: this device/user/path, time-bound, with owner and review date.
items.explain: Solve the workflow without permanent allow-all; record the exception properly.

items.prompt: Ticket: after a Network Control update, the backup server can't reach its targets. Scope check first?
items.answer: Confirm whether it's the backup server only or all machines under the updated policy, then correlate with the change log.
items.explain: Scope tells you whether the policy change or the server is the variable; check both sides.

items.prompt: Ticket: user is shouting that 'the security thing' deleted their files. They mean a quarantine. Your move?
items.answer: Acknowledge impact, check what was actually quarantined and why, restore if it's a false positive — fix first, explain second.
items.explain: Quarantine is recoverable; the customer's panic is the immediate problem to manage.

items.prompt: Customer: 'Just turn this thing off, it's costing me money.' Best response shape?
items.answer: 'I hear you — let's get you working right now, and I'll make sure this exact block doesn't happen again.' Then fix narrowly.
items.explain: Validate the cost concern, deliver the fix, and promise prevention — never debate the product's existence.

items.prompt: Executive: 'Why did this happen?' after you fixed their block. Answer in what language?
items.answer: Business-impact language: what happened, what you did, how long, what prevents recurrence. No architecture lecture.
items.explain: Executives want confidence and prevention, not a policy-architecture seminar.

items.prompt: User asks you to approve an app 'because my manager said it's fine.' Sufficient authorization?
items.answer: No — manager say-so is not binary verification. Verify the file, then approve on technical grounds.
items.explain: Social pressure is how malware gets approved. The verification workflow doesn't take verbal shortcuts.

items.prompt: After resolving an angry customer's ticket, what one line earns future trust?
items.answer: A plain-language explanation of why the block happened and what you changed so it won't recur.
items.explain: Understanding converts the angry customer into someone who defends the control next time.

items.prompt: You must tell a user their requested app is denied as unsafe. How?
items.answer: State the decision plainly, give the specific reason (unsigned, known-risk indicator), and offer the safe alternative path.
items.explain: A denied request with a reason and an alternative is service; a denied request with silence is obstruction.

handsOnLab.title: Run the 8-ticket timed shift
handsOnLab.brief: Execute the full Cyber Hero shift: 8 tickets, a running clock, the scored rubric. You will write a resolution for each ticket, score yourself against the rubric, and compare with the model resolutions.
steps: Create shift-log.md with sections: clock start, one section per ticket (T1-T8), and a score table.
Set a 90-minute timer for the whole shift. Log your start time.
T1 (blocked legit app): write your investigation steps and approval decision — binary verification, scope, and policy change — in under 12 minutes.
T2 (suspected malware): write your containment and escalation actions — what you isolate, what evidence you preserve, who you notify — in under 12 minutes.
T3 (elevation request): write the grant decision using the what/why/how-long/where framework — in under 10 minutes.
T4 (storage false positive): write the exception with owner, expiry, and review date — in under 10 minutes.
T5 (network-control outage): write the diagnosis order and the surgical fix (no module disable) — in under 12 minutes.
T6 (Detect alert): write the triage sequence and your close-or-escalate decision with reasoning — in under 10 minutes.
T7 (angry customer): write your exact de-escalation script — first three sentences verbatim — in under 8 minutes.
T8 (executive escalation): write the technical resolution plus the executive-language summary — in under 10 minutes.
Stop the clock. Score each ticket on the rubric: correctness 40, posture 25, communication 20, documentation 15.
Compare each resolution against the model resolutions in the notes; for any ticket under 70, rewrite it to the 100-point version.
Write a 5-line shift retrospective: what slowed you down, which ticket type needs more reps.
handsOnLab.deliverable: shift-log.md with 8 timestamped resolutions, rubric scores, and a retrospective.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: Every ticket has a resolution written inside its timebox, every ticket is scored on all four rubric factors, and any sub-70 ticket has a rewritten model-grade version.

videos.title: ThreatLocker YouTube channel — product walkthroughs and demos
videos.blurb: Official vendor channel with product walkthroughs and demos of the modules you triage against in this shift — watch an allowlisting and policy demo to ground the ticket scenarios.

mockTask.q: Panel-style question: a user calls, furious, because our agent blocked their application ten minutes into a client presentation. Walk us through your response, in order.
choices: Acknowledge the impact, verify the blocked binary, approve it narrowly if legitimate, confirm they're working, then explain the block plainly
Explain the zero-trust policy architecture first so they understand, then start troubleshooting
Disable the agent on their machine immediately to restore service, then investigate later
Tell them their admin configured the policy and transfer them to their IT department
mockTask.explain: Impact first, verification before approval, narrow scope, confirm resolution, then the plain-language explanation. Disabling the agent trades the whole control for one ticket; lecturing an angry user teaches nothing.

notes.title: Logistics: getting to 1950 W Maitland Blvd on time
notes.body:
The facts: Tuesday, October 13, 2026, 9:00 AM Eastern, 1950 W Maitland Blvd, Orlando, FL 32810 — IT Infrastructure Specialist, via Crawford Thomas recruiter Alex Starr. Your plan works backward from 9:00. Worked example timeline: target arrival 8:15-8:20 AM (40-45 minutes early — early enough to absorb traffic, not so early you hover). That means leaving home by roughly 7:15-7:30 depending on your drive; do a dry run of the route on a weekday morning before the 13th and time it, because Tuesday-morning Orlando traffic is not Sunday-afternoon traffic. Morning-of: depart with a 15-minute buffer on top of the dry-run time, phone fully charged, recruiter's number saved (Alex Starr at Crawford Thomas) in case of a genuine emergency delay. On arrival: park, sit in the car for five minutes, review your five questions for them and your two best STAR stories, then walk in at about 8:30 — 30 minutes early reads as professional, 45+ minutes early reads as anxious. Check in with the front desk, state your name, the 9:00 interview, and the role. Common mistakes: relying on GPS alone without a dry run (construction and school zones don't care about your interview), arriving exactly on time (one red light makes you late), and forgetting that '9:00 AM ET' in October means morning rush hour in Orlando. The dry run is the highest-value 40 minutes of your prep.

Worked example — the full timeline table. Night before: kit packed, clothes laid out, alarm set for 6:00 AM, recruiter number saved. 6:00 — wake, shower. 6:30 — protein breakfast, review the five questions and two STAR stories once. 7:00 — final check: kit, ID, phone charged. 7:15 — depart (dry-run time plus 15-minute buffer). 8:15 — arrive, park, five-minute car review. 8:30 — walk in, check in at front desk. 9:00 — interview. The delay contingency, rehearsed in advance so panic never decides: if traffic stops you, call Alex Starr the moment you know you'll be late — script: 'Hi Alex, this is Enmanuel Mejia, I'm on my way to the 9:00 interview but traffic on [road] has me about 15 minutes behind. I'm at [landmark]. I'll keep you posted.' One call, honest, specific. Then drive safely — speeding to an interview risks everything for nothing. Common mistake: texting instead of calling for a delay. A call shows respect; a text can sit unread. And never no-show silently — even a 30-minute delay handled professionally beats a disappearance. The plan assumes things go wrong; that's what makes it a plan.

notes.title: What to bring: the interview kit
notes.body:
Pack the night before — decision fatigue and rushing destroy mornings. Worked example kit list: (1) three printed copies of your tailored resume on clean paper, in a folder — panels often have more interviewers than expected; (2) a one-page reference sheet of your login-free portfolio highlights (your capstone defense plan and SOC playbook from M47/M48, summarized in three bullets each — you may not need them, but having them changes how you carry yourself); (3) a notebook and two pens — taking notes signals seriousness and gives your hands something to do; (4) a list of your five questions for them, printed or in the notebook; (5) government-issued photo ID; (6) a bottle of water; (7) your phone, silenced completely (not vibrate — silent), ideally left in the car or face-down in your bag. What NOT to bring: a laptop you don't need, strong fragrance, gum, or anything you have to juggle. The notebook does quiet double duty: when they describe the team's challenges, writing one line down shows you're processing, and it gives you material for the thank-you note. Operator gotcha: don't hand over your resume unprompted at the start — offer it ('I brought copies in case they're useful') and let them decide. You are a guest in their process; the kit exists so you're never the person saying 'I didn't bring one.'

Worked example — the portfolio one-pager. Title: 'Endpoint Security Work — Enmanuel Mejia.' Three bullets: 'Zero-Trust Defense Plan: designed a 150-endpoint ThreatLocker deployment for a healthcare clinic — tiered allowlisting, ringfencing, elevation control, phased 12-week rollout with gates (full document available).' 'AI-Augmented SOC Playbook: evaluation-gated AI triage workflow for a small team — four evaluation gates, human-in-the-loop approval points, honest metrics (full document available).' 'Live Triage Reps: 8-ticket timed simulation covering blocks, malware, elevation, storage, network, alerts, and escalations.' That's it — one page, no jargon walls. Notebook tactics: date the top of the page, write the interviewers' names as they introduce themselves (asking 'how do you spell that?' is fine), and capture one specific detail per person — you'll need those for the thank-you notes. When they describe a challenge, write 3-4 words ('lab rebuild — Q4'), then look back up — sustained eye contact matters more than transcription. After the interview, the notebook becomes your debrief source. Gotcha: don't read your questions off the page robotically — glance, then ask conversationally. Keep a backup pen in your bag — pens die at the worst moments, and asking to borrow one mid-interview is an avoidable stumble.

notes.title: Dress and first impressions for an infrastructure role
notes.body:
You're interviewing for an IT Infrastructure Specialist role at a cybersecurity company — the dress code target is sharp business casual leaning professional, not a suit and not a hoodie. Worked example: pressed chinos or dress slacks, a collared button-down shirt (tucked), clean closed-toe shoes, belt, minimal accessories. If you run warm, choose breathable fabric — Orlando in October is still warm and stress sweat is real. Grooming: neat hair, trimmed nails, clean-shaven or tidy facial hair. The first 90 seconds are disproportionately weighted: stand, firm handshake, eye contact, 'Good morning, I'm Enmanuel Mejia — thank you for having me.' Then let them lead. Body language for the panel: sit upright but not rigid, hands visible on the table or in your lap (not in pockets), nod while listening, and address the person who asked while glancing at the others. Common mistakes: overdressing into a full suit for a hands-on infrastructure role (it can read as not understanding the culture), underdressing (jeans signal you didn't prepare), and the nervous habits — pen clicking, leg bouncing, phone checking. Put the phone away before you enter the building. First impressions are set before the first technical question; make them boring in the best way — competent, calm, prepared.

Worked example — the first 90 seconds, scripted and rehearsed: stand as they approach, smile, firm handshake, eye contact: 'Good morning, I'm Enmanuel Mejia — thanks for having me in today.' When seated: 'I'm looking forward to this — I've spent the last few months going deep on zero-trust endpoint defense, so I'm excited to talk about the real work.' Then stop talking and let them lead. That opening does three jobs: name, gratitude, and a forward-leaning signal about the role's actual domain. Panel body language: when one person asks, answer to them but make eye contact with the others as you make key points — it keeps the whole panel engaged. If two people talk at once, smile and say 'you first' — small courtesies read as confidence. Hands: visible, still — on the table or in your lap. When you need a thinking second, say 'good question — let me think for a moment' rather than filling with 'um.' Silence while thinking looks thoughtful; filler while thinking looks nervous. The gotcha: mirroring nervous energy. If the panel is rapid-fire, stay at your pace — calm is contagious in both directions, and you want to be the source.

notes.title: Morning-of routine: energy, calm, timing
notes.body:
The morning of October 13 is execution, not preparation — all studying ends the night before. Worked example routine: wake at 6:00 AM (two full hours before departure buffer), shower, eat a real breakfast with protein (not just coffee — your brain burns glucose under stress), review only three things: your five questions for them, your two strongest STAR stories, and the drive route. No new material — cramming new facts at 7:30 AM only surfaces anxiety. Leave by your planned time with the buffer; in the car, listen to something calm or nothing at all, not a frantic podcast. Arrive 8:15-8:20, do the five-minute car review, walk in ~8:30. While waiting: breathe slowly, review your questions once more, and remind yourself of one true thing — you have done the reps (the triage sim, the capstones, the panel prep). If nerves spike in the room, the reset is physical: feet flat, slow exhale, sip water, then answer. Common mistakes: the all-nighter (sleep deprivation destroys recall and emotional regulation — a tired brain interviews 30% worse), skipping breakfast (hunger reads as irritability), and arriving with zero buffer so the whole morning is a sprint. You want to walk in slightly early, slightly bored, and completely ready — boredom is the feeling of a plan working.

The night-before checklist does more for your morning than willpower: kit packed and by the door, clothes laid out including shoes and belt, alarm set (plus a backup), coffee/breakfast ready to go, phone charging, car fueled or charged with the address already in navigation. Each item you handle tonight is one fewer decision under morning adrenaline. The physiology of nerves: a racing heart is adrenaline preparing you to perform — reinterpret it ('my body is getting ready') rather than fighting it, which research on stress reappraisal shows actually improves performance. The 4-count reset in the waiting room: inhale 4 counts, hold 4, exhale 4, twice — it measurably slows heart rate. Avoid the waiting-room traps: scrolling your phone (it fragments focus and the posture reads as disengaged), rehearsing answers frantically (you're prepared — trust the reps), and too much coffee (jittery hands, dry mouth, bathroom urgency mid-interview). One normal cup with breakfast is the dose. Walk in hydrated, fed, and slightly early — the physical basics are the foundation every technique stands on. Set out your water bottle with the kit the night before — dehydration dulls focus, and you will not want to hunt for water while the clock runs.

notes.title: Question-asking strategy: five smart questions for THEM
notes.body:
'Do you have questions for us?' is not a courtesy — it's the final scored section. Your five questions must show you understand the actual work of an IT Infrastructure Specialist at a zero-trust endpoint company. Worked examples: (1) 'What does the first 90 days look like for this role — what would a strong start accomplish?' (shows you think in outcomes); (2) 'How is the infrastructure team structured, and how does it work with the support and security teams day to day?' (shows you think in collaboration); (3) 'What's the biggest infrastructure challenge the team is facing right now?' (shows you want the real problems — listen hard, this is gold); (4) 'How does the team handle on-call or after-hours incidents?' (shows you understand operational reality); (5) 'What does growth look like from this role — what skills do the strongest people here develop?' (shows ambition with humility). Delivery rules: ask them conversationally, not as an interrogation; ask follow-ups on their answers ('You mentioned the team is rebuilding the lab environment — what's driving that?'); never ask about salary, benefits, or remote work in the first interview unless they raise it; and never ask something the website answers in ten seconds. The gotcha: 'No, I think you covered everything' — it reads as disinterest. Even if they answered everything, ask your best remaining question reframed: 'You touched on the team structure — could you say more about how the infrastructure side collaborates with support?'

Worked example follow-ups that show listening: they say the team is rebuilding the lab environment — you ask, 'What's driving the rebuild — new tooling, or scaling for more endpoints?' They mention on-call rotations — 'How are after-hours alerts triaged — is there a primary/secondary split?' Each follow-up proves you processed the answer, and their answers become thank-you-note material. Questions to never ask in round one, with reasons: salary and benefits (signals the job is a transaction — the recruiter handles compensation), 'how fast can I get promoted' (signals you're already looking past the role), anything answered on the website's careers page (signals zero research), and 'do you monitor employees' style adversarial questions (signals distrust). The meta-rule: every question should make them think 'this person understands the work.' A safe closer if time is short: 'What's the most important problem this role will help solve in the next six months?' — it ends the interview with them picturing you solving it. Write their answer down; it's the first line of your thank-you note.

notes.title: STAR delivery under pressure
notes.body:
Behavioral questions ('Tell me about a time when...') are scored on structure as much as content — STAR (Situation, Task, Action, Result) keeps a nervous brain from rambling. Worked example — 'Tell me about a time you dealt with a difficult user': Situation — 'At a previous support role, a department head's presentation laptop was blocked by our endpoint agent minutes before an all-hands.' Task — 'I needed to restore her access without weakening the security policy.' Action — 'I verified the blocked application by hash, confirmed it was legitimate, approved it scoped to her machine, and stayed on the line while she tested.' Result — 'She presented on time, and I documented the exception so the block wouldn't recur.' Then the closer most candidates skip: the lesson — 'It taught me that speed and verification aren't opposites — you do both, in order.' Keep each STAR to 90-120 seconds; longer and you lose the panel. Prepare five stories that cover: a difficult user, a mistake you made, a time you learned something fast, a disagreement with a colleague, and a time you improved a process. The gotcha: fictional polish. Never invent history — draw on real experience (your labs, your projects, your real work), and it's fine to say 'in a lab environment I built...' Honesty about being junior with strong fundamentals beats a fabricated senior war story that collapses under one follow-up question.

Second worked example — the mistake story, fully built: Situation — 'Early in a support role, I approved an application block exception by filename without verifying the hash — I was rushing to clear a queue.' Task — 'The app turned out to be a renamed unwanted program, and I had to own the error.' Action — 'I immediately revoked the exception, quarantined the file, told my lead exactly what I'd done before they found it, and wrote myself a verification checklist.' Result — 'Nothing spread, but I learned the expensive way.' The lesson closer — 'Since then I verify by hash or publisher every time, no matter how loud the queue is — speed never outranks verification.' Notice the structure: no excuses, self-reported, concrete fix, durable lesson. Timing practice: record each story on your phone and check it's 90-120 seconds — most people discover their 'two-minute' story is actually four. Cut ruthlessly: one situation sentence, one task sentence, two action sentences, one result, one lesson. If a story runs long in the room, land the plane: '...and the lesson was X.' A clean landing beats a perfect story that never ends.

notes.title: Thank-you note template and post-interview debrief
notes.body:
Send the thank-you within 24 hours — same day is best. Worked example template: Subject: 'Thank you — IT Infrastructure Specialist interview.' Body: 'Hi [Name], Thank you for your time today — I enjoyed our conversation about [specific thing they mentioned, e.g., the team's lab rebuild]. I'm excited about the IT Infrastructure Specialist role because [one genuine reason tied to what you learned]. [One-line reinforcement: e.g., My background in endpoint triage and zero-trust policy work maps directly onto the challenges you described.] Thanks again, and please let me know if I can provide anything else. Best, Enmanuel Mejia, [phone].' Send one per interviewer if you have names/addresses (ask the recruiter, Alex Starr, for the right contacts), each with a different specific detail — never a mass BCC. Then the debrief checklist, done the same evening while memory is fresh: (1) write down every question they asked and your answer's weak spots; (2) note names, titles, and one personal detail per interviewer; (3) record what excited you and what worried you about the role; (4) list any follow-up you promised ('I'll send that lab writeup'); (5) email the recruiter a brief status note. Then stop — no second-guessing spirals, no 'should I have said.' You executed the plan; the outcome is data, not a verdict on your worth.

Filled example — the thank-you note with specifics: Subject: 'Thank you — IT Infrastructure Specialist interview.' Body: 'Hi [Name], Thank you for your time today — I particularly enjoyed hearing about the lab rebuild and how the infrastructure team partners with support on escalations. I'm excited about the IT Infrastructure Specialist role because the zero-trust endpoint work is exactly where I've focused my preparation, and the team's challenges are the kind I want to help solve. Please let me know if I can provide anything else — my portfolio documents are ready to share if useful. Best, Enmanuel Mejia, [phone].' Each interviewer gets a different specific callback (lab rebuild for one, on-call structure for another). The recruiter status note, same evening: 'Hi Alex, today's interview went well — I enjoyed meeting [names]. Thank you for setting it up. Please let me know the next steps whenever you hear.' Short, professional, grateful. Then the debrief form: questions asked (verbatim as you remember), your weak spots (be brutally honest — this is for you), names/titles/one detail each, what excited you, what worried you, promised follow-ups. File it. The interview is over; the system you built for the next one just got better.
